questions.q: Why can't a single Terraform resource block conditionally become either azurerm_virtual_network or aws_vpc at apply time?
options: A resource block's type is fixed in the configuration; the branching has to happen at the resource-selection level instead, not inside one resource
Terraform does not allow declaring both the azurerm and aws providers in the same configuration
Only one provider can ever appear in a required_providers block
Resource blocks can only be used with the azurerm provider, never with aws
questions.explain: A resource block's type (e.g. azurerm_virtual_network) is fixed; it can never transform into a different resource type like aws_vpc at apply time. Multi-cloud modules branch by conditionally creating zero or one of each resource, not by mutating one resource into another.

questions.q: In the count-per-cloud pattern shown in this lesson, what does `count = var.cloud == "azure" ? 1 : 0` actually do?
options: It deletes the aws_vpc resource from the Terraform registry
It creates exactly one instance of that resource when var.cloud is "azure", and zero instances (so it doesn't exist in state) otherwise
It always creates exactly one instance of the resource regardless of var.cloud's value
It duplicates the resource across both clouds simultaneously
questions.explain: count evaluates to 1 or 0 based on the cloud variable; when it's 0, Terraform creates zero instances of that resource block, so only the matching cloud's branch actually provisions anything.

questions.q: What is the actual portability payoff of giving a multi-cloud module a unified output like `network_id`?
options: It makes the Terraform state file smaller
It removes the need for a cloud variable entirely
It automatically migrates existing resources from one cloud to another
Calling code that uses the module doesn't need its own cloud == "azure" branch, because the module already normalized the attribute name regardless of which cloud produced it
questions.explain: The output block maps either azurerm_virtual_network.this[0].id or aws_vpc.this[0].id to the same network_id name, so modules consuming this one don't need to know or care which cloud actually created the network.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend composing multi-cloud logic as child modules rather than inlining both clouds' resources with ternaries throughout a flat configuration?
options: Child modules run faster at apply time than flat configurations
Terraform requires child modules for any configuration with more than one provider
It keeps the cloud-branching logic contained and reviewable in one place instead of spreading var.cloud == "azure" ? ... : ... ternaries through every resource
Child modules are the only way to declare a variable named cloud
questions.explain: Nesting the count-per-cloud pattern inside dedicated child modules, with var.cloud threaded down once from the root, keeps a multi-cloud codebase maintainable instead of scattering conditionals through every resource.

questions.q: When would you reach for provider aliasing (e.g. `provider = aws.secondary`) instead of the count-per-cloud pattern?
options: When you want to rename a resource without changing its type
When you never intend to use more than one cloud
When you want Terraform to automatically pick whichever cloud is cheaper
When a single apply genuinely needs to create resources on both clouds at once, rather than conditionally choosing one
questions.explain: Provider aliasing is for the different scenario where both resources should exist on every apply — no conditional at all, just two providers and two resources living in the same state.
